findings.paper_title: Item 08 - Appendix 1 - Guildford Corporate Performance_report_Q1_202627
findings.headline: Guildford cannot demonstrate five-year housing supply after NPPF housing need requirement doubled from 562 to 1,168 dwellings per annum in April 2025
findings.detail: The council's required annual housing delivery increased sharply following April 2025 NPPF changes. It has failed to meet the new requirement (only 367 units delivered in 2025/26 against target of 1,166, then only 27 units in Q1 2026/27 against 292 target). The council cannot now evidence a five-year housing supply, which automatically triggers NPPF presumption in favour of sustainable development and requires compliance testing against the Housing Delivery Test. The council expects to underperform the HDT 75% threshold and acknowledges it will take several years to comply while a new Local Plan is prepared.
findings.matters: A council unable to demonstrate housing supply loses planning control and faces developer-friendly presumptions. This affects the council's strategic positioning, regeneration income, and planning authority credibility.
findings.figures: Housing need increased 562 to 1,168 dwellings per annum; 367 delivered vs 1,166 target in 2025/26; 27 units vs 292 target in Q1; cumulative shortfall 1,145 dwellings over three-year period; only 1,441 units delivered vs 2,457 required for 95% HDT threshold
findings.quote: Following changes to the National Planning Policy Framework (NPPF) in 2024, Guildford's local housing need increased from 562 to 1,168 dwellings per annum. Since 1 April 2025 the Council has been unable to demonstrate a five-year housing land supply. This has triggered the NPPF presumption in favour of sustainable development, meaning planning applications are assessed under the 'tilted balance' where relevant.

findings.figures: £1–£2 per week potential additional rent per property
findings.quote: We estimate that the Council's current rent levels are below the 'formula rent' and that the anticipated impact is an increase of approximately £1–£2 per week for tenants, on top of the standard rent increase. Further work will be undertaken to review impacts once the consultation response is released and any proposals will be made for the 2027/28 budget.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 - HRA Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: £167m external HRA debt with no repayment priority in the business plan
findings.detail: The council carries £167m in external borrowing from the 2012 self-financing settlement. The business plan 'attach[es] a lower priority to the repayment of debt principal', choosing instead to fund affordable housing investment. With £77m in HRA reserves, this is deliberate policy rather than financial stress.
findings.matters: High levels of unrepaid debt and the policy drivers behind it matter for credit assessment and understanding long-term financial commitments.
findings.figures: £167m external debt; £77m HRA reserves estimated 31 March 2026
findings.quote: The estimates, consistent with the Business Plan, continue to attach a lower priority to the repayment of debt principal inherited as part of the self-financing HRA settlement, reflecting the Council's determination to provide new additional affordable homes and increase the investment in housing stock.

findings.paper_title: Item 10 - HRA Budget 2026-27
findings.headline: Maintenance backlog being caught up with £12m capital programme increase
findings.detail: The council fell behind on maintenance work in recent years and is now prioritizing catch-up. The capital budget has increased to £12m to 'help redress' the shortfall in maintenance on the 5,200-home stock.
findings.matters: A lender needs assurance that housing stock is properly maintained; deferred maintenance creates long-term cost and liability risks.
findings.figures: £12m capital programme increase for 2026/27
findings.quote: The last few years have presented unique challenges for managing our housing stock and as a result we have been unable to undertake all the work that we would have expected to the homes we manage. This budget continues with the work started over the past two years to help redress that issue.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 (9) - GF Budget Setting 2026 - App 9 - Section 25 CFO Report
findings.headline: The new unitary council will require future savings to remain solvent, but the CFO provides no quantum or delivery plan.
findings.detail: In the Future Outlook section, the CFO identifies savings delivery as a key requirement but does not specify the scale of required savings or how these will be achieved. The 2026-27 budget itself is confirmed as prudent and balanced, but the statement about future savings indicates financial pressure beyond the current budget year.
findings.matters: Unspecified future savings requirements signal budget pressures ahead for the new entity; lenders need visibility of savings quantum and delivery plans to assess financial sustainability post-reorganisation.
findings.figures: No figures provided for required savings; reorganisation costs built into 2026-27 budget
findings.quote: Future savings will be required to ensure the new council remains solvent and can take advantage of the transformation opportunities

findings.paper_title: Item 11 (9) - GF Budget Setting 2026 - App 9 - Section 25 CFO Report
findings.headline: External audits for 2021-22 and 2022-23 remain incomplete due to national backlog, with disclaimer opinions issued in their place.
findings.detail: Grant Thornton has audited 2024-25 accounts but has not completed audits for 2021-22 and 2022-23. These accounts have been 'backstopped' with disclaimer audit opinions, meaning no formal audit conclusion on the financial statements for a two-year period. While the CFO states controls are sufficient, this creates a gap in independently verified financial data during a key period.
findings.matters: Lenders depend on verified historical financial statements to assess council financial health; unaudited accounts prevent independent confirmation of the financial position and control environment.
findings.figures: 2021-22 and 2022-23 accounts with disclaimer audit opinions; 2024-25 audit completed
findings.quote: Due to the national backlog, Grant Thornton have not undertaken audits of the 2021-22 and 2022-23 accounts, and these have been 'backstopped' and a disclaimer audit opinion issued on them.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 (9) - GF Budget Setting 2026 - App 9 - Section 25 CFO Report
findings.headline: Local government reorganisation will merge Guildford into a new unitary council from 1 April 2027, with uncertainty about the partner councils' financial circumstances.
findings.detail: Guildford and five other Surrey councils will merge into two new unitary councils from April 2027. The CFO explicitly flags uncertainty about partner councils' financial health as a medium-term risk factor for the new entity. A Voluntary Joint Committee and Shadow Unitary Council are being formed, and significant reorganisation work is underway. The date is confirmed by government decision in October 2025.
findings.matters: Structural reorganisation of this scale introduces operational and financial risk; partner councils' viability is critical to the new entity's starting position and future borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: Merger effective date: 1 April 2027; decision date: October 2025
findings.quote: There is currently significant uncertainty beyond the 2026-27 budget due to the formation of the new unitary council and the existing financial circumstances of our proposed partners.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 - GF Budget Setting Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Acolaid system replacement requires £330k in 2026/27, with £1m needed over the full project life
findings.detail: A critical planning and building control system (used by Planning, Land Charges and Building Control) will cease to be supported in the near future and must be replaced. A business case is still being developed for the full project.
findings.matters: Aging IT infrastructure represents hidden capital risk. A £1m replacement cost for a system without a complete business case yet signals either deferred investment or incomplete planning.
findings.figures: £330k growth in 2026/27; £1m total requirement across project life
findings.quote: This includes £330k for the Acolaid system, which has been used by Planning, Land Charges and Building Control for a number of years but will cease to be supported in the near future. The growth bid across the years totals £1m and a full business case is required for the project to proceed.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 - GF Budget Setting Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Pension cost increase of £212k due to methodology change from fixed sum to payroll-percentage basis
findings.detail: The council's back-funded pension element (extra funding to cover past shortfalls) is now calculated as a percentage of payroll rather than a fixed sum. This is a recurring cost increase driven by contractual change, not discretionary spend.
findings.matters: Employment-related costs are rising and will recur annually. The change from fixed to variable cost structure means future pension contributions will scale with pay increases.
findings.figures: £212k additional budget requirement for pension changes
findings.quote: Following a change in how the back funded element of pension payments is calculated, moving from a fixed sum to a percentage change based on the payroll, there is an additional budget requirement of £212k.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 - GF Budget Setting Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Medium-term plan projects continued financial pressures through 2029/30, despite current balance
findings.detail: While 2026/27 is balanced and 2027/28 is claimed to be in balance within the MTFP, the council explicitly states the plan 'continues to project future financial pressures' beyond that horizon. Reserves are currently stable but future years remain uncertain.
findings.matters: Lenders assess multi-year sustainability. A balanced budget now with declared future pressures ahead suggests the council has deferred rather than solved underlying structural problems.
findings.figures: MTFP covers 2026/27 to 2029/30; balanced over next two years
findings.quote: the latest MTFP for the years ending 2029/30 continues to project future financial pressures. The Council is taking action to ensure sufficient funding is in place to deliver and maintain services for 2026/27, but this report also explains the conditions and uncertainties that will impact service delivery in future years.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 - GF Budget Setting Report 2026-27
findings.headline: £822,648 in Local Government Reorganisation transition costs for 2026/27, ahead of unitary authority formation in 2027/28
findings.detail: Guildford is combining with Waverley to form a new West Surrey Unitary Authority. The budget includes a direct cost contribution for one-off integration, IT harmonisation, governance restructuring, and staffing alignment. Councils are preparing for a major structural change.
findings.matters: Reorganisation creates operational disruption risk, cost overruns, and management distraction during a critical transition. The council is also extracting financial data to form the foundation for the new authority.
findings.figures: Guildford Borough Council will directly contribute £822,648 in 2026/27; joint budget challenge boards held with Waverley
findings.quote: Transition Costs: LGR will involve significant one-off costs, such as integrating services, aligning governance structures, and harmonising IT systems and staffing arrangements. The MTFP will ensure that adequate resources are allocated for these transitional expenses while protecting core service delivery. Guildford Borough Council will directly contribute £822,648 in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 - GF Budget Setting Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Waste & Recycling income of £420k has been written off as 'no longer achievable'
findings.detail: The council has removed a previously expected income target from the budget because the projected income can no longer be realised. This is a concrete income failure requiring budget adjustment, not a projection.
findings.matters: A demonstrable shortfall in a service income stream signals either declining activity, market failure, or planning error. It reduces discretionary resources.
findings.figures: £420k adjustment to Waste & Recycling income target
findings.quote: A £420k adjustment to the Waste & Recycling income target, as the projected income is no longer achievable and needs to be removed from the budget.

findings.paper_title: Item 11 - GF Budget Setting Report 2026-27
findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision jumps by £937k in a single year, the largest budget growth item
findings.detail: MRP is the amount set aside to repay outstanding capital borrowing. A £937k increase represents a step change in debt servicing costs. The council has a £10.9m borrowing requirement over the next three years against a three-year capital programme of £11.1m.
findings.matters: A major increase in debt repayment obligations is a significant fixed cost that will persist across future years, reducing financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £937k increase in MRP for 2026/27; £10.9m borrowing requirement attached to three-year capital bids of £11.1m
findings.quote: A significant portion of this growth is due to the £937k increase in the Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) for 2026/27. The MRP is the amount a local authority must set aside each year to cover the cost of its outstanding borrowing for capital projects, ensuring that debt is repaid gradually rather than deferred to future years.

findings.paper_title: Item 09 (2) - Capital Strategy 2026-27 - App 2 - Treasury Man Strategy
findings.headline: HRA debt declining steadily from £150m to £110m over five years with no new external borrowing planned
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account external debt is on a fixed downward trajectory from £150m in 2024 to £110m by 2029-30. No additional external borrowing is planned for the HRA. This self-financing debt originates from the £184m borrowed in 2012 to fund the HRA self-financing buyout, with £5m met internally.
findings.matters: Predictable debt reduction improves the council's long-term fiscal position and shows disciplined repayment of legacy financing commitments. Relevant to overall council financial stability.
findings.figures: HRA external debt 2023-24: £159m | 2026-27: £131m | 2029-30: £110m | Original 2012 borrowing: £184m | Internal contribution 2012: £5m
findings.quote: The HRA self-financing implementation required the HRA to pay the Government £189m in March 2012. The Council borrowed £184m in March 2012 for this purpose with £5m being met by an internal loan. The outstanding debt as at the 31 March 2024 will be £150m

findings.paper_title: Item 09 (2) - Capital Strategy 2026-27 - App 2 - Treasury Man Strategy
findings.headline: Guildford is deliberately under-borrowed, funding capital spending from reserves rather than external debt
findings.detail: Despite having a General Fund capital financing requirement (CFR) of £40m in 2026-27, the council holds zero external debt and funds £49.6m of its £91.4m capital programme through internal borrowing (drawing on reserves and balances). The under-borrowed position is projected to widen to £81m by 2027-28. This is a deliberate strategy stated as 'prudent' because investment returns are low and counterparty risk is uncertain.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand refinancing risk and how long the council can sustain capital spending from reserves before external borrowing becomes necessary. A tightening cash position would force a shift to external markets.
findings.figures: General Fund CFR 2026-27: £40m | External debt 2026-27: £0m | Under-borrowed position: £76m | Internal borrowing in capital financing 2026-27: £49.6m | Total capital expenditure 2026-27: £91.4m
findings.quote: The Council is currently maintaining an under-borrowed position. This means that the capital borrowing need (the Capital Financing Requirement), has not been fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Council's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as a temporary measure. This strategy is prudent as treasury management investment returns are low and counterparty risk is still uncertain.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026-27 - App 2 - Treasury Management Strategy
findings.headline: Council holds commercial property portfolio but commits to review exits if external borrowing becomes necessary
findings.detail: The council states it has an existing commercial property portfolio and is not required to sell it. However, the Prudential Code requires review of exits 'should the Council have an expected need to borrow'. This hedging language suggests the portfolio is recognized as a potential source of liquidity if the under-borrowed position becomes untenable.
findings.matters: The portfolio is implicitly listed as a contingent financing tool. Fire-sales of commercial property into adverse market conditions could lock in losses.
findings.figures: Commercial property portfolio holdings not quantified in this document
findings.quote: The Council has an existing commercial property portfolio that it is not required by the Prudential Code to sell. However, should the Council have an expected need to borrow, the Prudential Code requires the Council to review options for exiting commercial property investments where these can be reasonably realised, based on a financial performance appraisal which takes account of financial implications and risk reduction benefits.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026-27 - App 2 - Treasury Management Strategy
findings.headline: Council has under-borrowed position of £52-81m but plans no external borrowing to close it
findings.detail: Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) exceeds external debt by £52-81m across the forecast period, meaning the council has unfinanced capital need. However, zero external borrowing is planned. Instead, this need is met by internal borrowing (drawing cash). The strategy is justified as prudent due to low investment returns, but creates dependency on maintaining reserve balances.
findings.matters: This posture is unusually defensive and cash-constrained. It leaves no borrowing headroom for unexpected capital needs or revenue pressures without forcing external borrowing at rates negotiated during stress.
findings.figures: CFR-GF 2026-27 £40m vs External Debt £0; Under/over external borrowing -£76m (2026-27) to -£81m (2027-28)
findings.quote: The Council is currently maintaining an under-borrowed position. This means that the capital borrowing need (the Capital Financing Requirement), has not been fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Council's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as a temporary measure. This strategy is prudent as treasury management investment returns are low and counterparty risk is still uncertain.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026-27 - App 2 - Treasury Management Strategy
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account financing costs rising from 38% to 46% of net revenue despite falling debt
findings.detail: HRA debt is declining as planned (£150m in 2023-24 to £110m forecast 2027-28), but HRA financing costs are rising in absolute terms (£12.3m to £16.4m) and as a percentage of net revenue (38% to 46%). This deteriorating ratio indicates cash flow pressure within the HRA despite debt reduction.
findings.matters: HRA financing costs above 40% constrain the ability to invest in maintenance and new housing. Rising pressure to 46% signals tightening headroom for service delivery.
findings.quote: Housing Revenue Account 12.3 13.3 14.3 15.3 16.4 [financing costs]. Housing Revenue Account 38% 38% 41% 44% 46% [as % of revenue]

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026-27 - App 2 - Treasury Management Strategy
findings.headline: Council financing 54-85% of capital spending from internal cash reserves rather than external borrowing
findings.detail: Internal Borrowing accounts for £94.2m of £110.5m total capex in 2025-26, and £49.6m of £91.4m in 2026-27. The council is deliberately drawing down cash reserves to fund capital instead of accessing the PWLB or other external sources. External borrowing is forecast at £0 for all five years despite a theoretical borrowing need (CFR).
findings.matters: This strategy depletes the reserve buffer and depends entirely on sufficient cash remaining available. Any unexpected outflow or revenue shortfall forces external borrowing at market rates, likely higher than PWLB.
findings.figures: Internal Borrowing 2025-26 £94,172k; 2026-27 £49,568k; External Borrowing £0 all years; CFR-GF rising from £14m to £40m
findings.quote: Internal Borrowing 94,172 [2025-26]... 49,568 [2026-27]... External Borrowing 0 0 0 0 0... The Council is currently maintaining an under-borrowed position... cash supporting the Council's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as a temporary measure.

findings.paper_title: Capital Strategy 2026-27 - App 2 - Treasury Management Strategy
findings.headline: General Fund capital spending collapses from £102.9m to £25.5m in four years
findings.detail: The capital expenditure forecast shows General Fund spending falling 75% from £102.9m in 2025-26 to £25.5m by 2028-29, then rising only slightly to £28.7m by 2029-30. This is a sharp, sustained decline, not a temporary dip. The document does not explain why this is happening.
findings.matters: A three-quarter reduction in capital investment signals either major project deferrals, completion of a prior catch-up programme, or resource constraint. Lenders need to understand which.
findings.quote: The estimates of capital expenditure the Council plans to incur during the forthcoming financial years are: [General Fund] 102,949,994 [2025/26]... 65,624,976 [2026/27]... 25,501,189 [2028/29]

findings.paper_title: Item 09 (2) - Statement of Accounts - App 2 - Audit Findings Report 2024-25 FINAL
findings.headline: Approximately 20% of audit samples at end of December 2025 could not be concluded on due to quality issues
findings.detail: The auditors note: 'approximately 20% of samples at the end of December 2025 could not be concluded on as they did not meet the required quality threshold.' This indicates systemic issues with the quality of evidence and record-keeping across the council's accounts preparation.
findings.matters: A 20% failure rate on audit samples is significant and suggests the council's financial controls and record-keeping are materially weak. This increases the risk that errors exist throughout the financial statements.
findings.figures: 20% of samples unable to be concluded as at end of December 2025
findings.quote: However, further work is required by the Council to ensure, high set of quality accounts, robust working papers, adequate and appropriate evidence being provided and reducing the audit timeframe ahead of the revised backstop dates in 25/26 and 26/27. The issues noted resulted in a high volume of audit queries and follow-ups, and approximately 20% of samples at the end of December 2025 could not be concluded on as they did not meet the required quality threshold.

findings.paper_title: Item 09 (2) - Statement of Accounts - App 2 - Audit Findings Report 2024-25 FINAL
findings.headline: Pension liability shows £14.8m after asset ceiling adjustment; prior-period restatement not explained in draft accounts
findings.detail: The pension IAS 19 liability is £14.8m after applying IFRIC 14 (asset ceiling adjustment). The draft accounts originally showed a net pension asset position (unusual) but management had not explained why. The draft accounts also contained a prior period restatement for pension liability 'but the accounts did not explain reason for adjusting the opening position.' Disclosure of estimation uncertainty requires enhancement.
findings.matters: Pension liabilities are sensitive to actuarial assumptions (discount rate, salary growth, mortality). A net liability position with a prior-period adjustment that is not explained suggests potential governance gaps in oversight of pension accounting.
findings.figures: £14.8m net pension liability at 31 March 2025 (prior year £10m liability); asset ceiling adjustment applied
findings.quote: The Council was showing a net pension asset position (as opposed to a net liability). In a net asset position, management had to consider the requirements of IFRIC 14. IFRIC 14 limits the extent to which a defined benefit net asset can be recognised. Management shared the IFRIC 14 assessment with us in November 2025 and our review noted a net liability should be recognised as result of the asset ceiling adjustment. In addition, the Draft Accounts also had a prior period restatement for Pension Liability/Opening Balance but the accounts did not explain reason for adjusting the opening position.

findings.paper_title: Item 09 (2) - Statement of Accounts - App 2 - Audit Findings Report 2024-25 FINAL
findings.headline: Investment Properties valued at £169.3m; 2 of 13 samples unable to be concluded on due to lack of supporting evidence
findings.detail: Investment property valuations are significant at £169.3m (nearly 10% of total assets). The auditors tested 13 samples and cleared 11, but for 2 samples: 'this was due to lack of adequate support for the key inputs that were used in the valuation i.e. rent agreements, comparables, etc.'
findings.matters: Investment properties are income-generating assets critical to understanding the Council's financial sustainability. Inability to verify 15% of samples tested suggests weak controls over the evidence supporting valuations, which are highly judgmental.
findings.figures: £169.3m total investment properties; 2 of 13 samples (15%) unable to conclude
findings.quote: We sample tested 13 samples and cleared 11. For the 2 samples we were unable to conclude, this was due to lack of adequate support for the key inputs that were used in the valuation i.e. rent agreements, comparables, etc.

findings.paper_title: Item 09 (2) - Statement of Accounts - App 2 - Audit Findings Report 2024-25 FINAL
findings.headline: Opening balances have not been rolled forward in Business World ledger for several years
findings.detail: When the Council implemented Business World in 2020, it did not roll forward opening balances for subsequent years. This fundamental control weakness meant: 'the quality of listings provided, particularly for balance sheet transactions, opening balances, and reconciliation of the trial balance to the financial statements' was poor. 'In some instances, the core statements did not reconcile to the relevant disclosure notes.'
findings.matters: Rolling forward opening balances is a basic ledger control. The failure to do this for several years has created a cascading uncertainty about the accuracy of the balance sheet, reserves, and prior-year comparatives. This affects both current-year decisions and historical trend analysis.
findings.figures: Issue spans from 2020 to 2024/25 (at least 4 years); affects balance sheet and disclosure notes reconciliations
findings.quote: When we commenced fieldwork, the Council had still not rolled forward (within Business World – new ledger implemented in 2020) its opening balances for several years. This impacted the quality of listings provided, particularly for balance sheet transactions, opening balances, and reconciliation of the trial balance to the financial statements.

findings.paper_title: Item 09 (2) - Statement of Accounts - App 2 - Audit Findings Report 2024-25 FINAL
findings.headline: IFRS 16 implementation incomplete; auditors unable to conclude on the impact to the financial statements
findings.detail: IFRS 16 (leases accounting standard) became effective 1 April 2024. The Council did not include an IFRS 16 impact assessment in its draft accounts. 'Officers subsequently completed an IFRS 16 assessment during the course of the audit, but this was not fully complete and compliant with the new standard. Due to the constraints of the backstop and incomplete working papers on IFRS 16, we have not undertaken substantive procedures on this balance.'
findings.matters: IFRS 16 requires recognition of right-of-use assets and lease liabilities on the balance sheet that were previously off-balance-sheet. For councils with significant lease or PFI arrangements, this can be material. The Council's failure to assess impact upfront and the auditors' inability to conclude means the accounts may not reflect all lease liabilities.
findings.figures: Previous disclosure (unaudited 2023/24) showed IFRS 16 impact of £11k general fund and £318k balance sheet
findings.quote: The Council's draft accounts presented for audit, did not have an IFRS 16 impact assessment. Officers subsequently completed an IFRS 16 assessment during the course of the audit, but this was not fully complete and compliant with the new standard. Due to the constraints of the backstop and incomplete working papers on IFRS 16, we have not undertaken substantive procedures on this balance.

findings.paper_title: Item 09 (2) - Statement of Accounts - App 2 - Audit Findings Report 2024-25 FINAL
findings.headline: Staff turnover and temporary finance team members have left the Council, hampering audit evidence and governance
findings.detail: The audit report notes: 'Officers involved in the field struggled to provide clear audit trails and explanations for these adjustments as they were prepared by different temporary finance team members who had left the Council.' This staff turnover has affected both the quality of audit evidence and the Council's own ability to explain its accounts.
findings.matters: High staff turnover in finance increases the risk of errors going undetected, weakens institutional knowledge, and makes it harder for the Council to respond to audit queries or lender requests. It also suggests either morale or capacity issues.
findings.figures: No specific numbers given; identified as affecting multiple temporary staff members across the audit
findings.quote: Officers involved in the field struggled to provide clear audit trails and explanations for these adjustments as they were prepared by different temporary finance team members who had left the Council.

findings.paper_title: Item 09 (2) - Statement of Accounts - App 2 - Audit Findings Report 2024-25 FINAL
findings.headline: Fixed Asset Register discrepancies: £21.2m gross and £20.9m net incorrectly tagged, affecting transparency of revaluation programme
findings.detail: Auditors identified: 'Assets with a gross book value of £21.2m and net book value of £20.9m were marked as revalued but not included in the valuation report. Additionally, three assets tagged as historic cost were revalued during the year.' While management explained this was due to prior period adjustments, it shows control weaknesses in the FAR.
findings.matters: The Fixed Asset Register is the foundation of property accounting. Discrepancies and incorrect tagging mean the Council may not have visibility of which assets have been properly revalued, which is critical for ensuring all material assets are carried at current value.
findings.figures: £21.2m gross book value and £20.9m net book value incorrectly tagged
findings.quote: Assets with a gross book value of £21.2m and net book value of £20.9m were marked as revalued but not included in the valuation report. Additionally, three assets tagged as historic cost were revalued during the year. These differences affect only the rolling programme disclosure, not the balance sheet.

findings.paper_title: Item 09 (2) - Statement of Accounts - App 2 - Audit Findings Report 2024-25 FINAL
findings.headline: Assets not revalued during the year; £3.95m variance identified and considered material
findings.detail: Assets that were not revalued in the year (£93m of the £242m other land and buildings) were assessed for impairment. The auditors performed their own assessment and identified 'a variance of £3.95m, which is material.' The Council had not done its own assessment: 'Management had not performed their own assessment of assets not revalued, and have relied on the valuer's assessment.'
findings.matters: On a rolling revaluation programme, the Council must assess whether assets not yet revalued may have been impaired. The auditors finding a material variance suggests the Council's assurance processes over a significant portion of assets are weak.
findings.figures: £3.95m variance identified; £93m of properties not revalued in year
findings.quote: Management had not performed their own assessment of assets not revalued, and have relied on the valuer's assessment. As such, we have performed our own assessment, where we note a variance of £3.95m, which is material.

findings.paper_title: Item 09 (2) - Statement of Accounts - App 2 - Audit Findings Report 2024-25 FINAL
findings.headline: Unable to obtain assurance on Depreciated Replacement Cost valuations; £11.6m variance identified in 5 assets tested
findings.detail: For assets valued using DRC (typically specialised buildings like libraries), the auditors could not obtain adequate supporting evidence. They tested 5 DRC assets and found 'a variance of £11.6m'. Management had not provided essential inputs: 'We are unable to obtain assurance over the (DRC and EUV) samples selected as we did not receive adequate supporting evidence for the inputs such as GIA, site plans, build costs, comparables, etc.'
findings.matters: DRC assets (£95m of the £242m land and buildings balance) are highly sensitive to assumptions about build costs and are difficult to value. The inability to verify them and discovery of material variances suggests the £95m valuation may not be reliable, affecting both the balance sheet and the council's borrowing capacity calculations.
findings.figures: £11.6m variance for 5 DRC assets tested; DRC assets total £95m
findings.quote: We are unable to obtain assurance over the (DRC and EUV) samples selected as we did not receive adequate supporting evidence for the inputs such as GIA, site plans, build costs, comparables, etc. We had to undertake alternative audit procedures for checking the build costs, However this resulted in a variance of £11.6m for the 5 DRC assets tested we reviewed.

findings.paper_title: Item 09 (2) - Statement of Accounts - App 2 - Audit Findings Report 2024-25 FINAL
findings.headline: Property and Equipment balance sheet did not reconcile with underlying note; £17.3m understatement identified
findings.detail: The balance sheet for Land and Buildings did not reconcile with the Property, Plant & Equipment disclosure note. The auditors identified that 'The draft PPE balance sheet amount was understated by £17.3m.' This suggests either incomplete recording of assets or errors in the trial balance to financial statements reconciliation.
findings.matters: Property typically represents the largest asset class on a council's balance sheet (here £242m + £603m + £169.3m in investment properties). A £17.3m error indicates weak controls over the fixed asset register and financial reporting process. This undermines the reliability of asset valuations and borrowing capacity calculations.
findings.figures: £17.3m understatement in draft PPE; total property and buildings valued at £242m (other), £603m (council housing), £169.3m (investment property)
findings.quote: The balance sheet did not reconcile with the PPE note. Management acknowledged this issue and agreed to amend the accounts to ensure internal consistency. The draft PPE balance sheet amount was understated by £17.3m.

findings.paper_title: Item 09 (2) - Statement of Accounts - App 2 - Audit Findings Report 2024-25 FINAL
findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision at 1.2% versus benchmarked 2% indicates under-provision and long-term financial sustainability risk
findings.detail: The Council's MRP charge (the amount set aside annually to repay borrowing) is 1.2% of the Capital Financing Requirement, compared to the typical local government benchmark of 2%. The auditors note: 'The Council's position indicates potential under-provision and long-term financial sustainability risks.' This means the Council is not setting aside enough each year to cover its debt repayment obligations.
findings.matters: Under-provision of MRP means the Council is deferring debt repayment obligations into future years. For a lender, this signals that forecast cash positions in future years may be overstated and that financial flexibility may be constrained.
findings.figures: MRP at 1.2% of closing Capital Financing Requirement; benchmark is 2%
findings.quote: The Council's Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) charge continues to be 1.2% of its closing Capital Financing Requirement in the preceding year. We typically consider a benchmark of 2% within the local government sector. The Council's position indicates potential under-provision and long-term financial sustainability risks.

findings.paper_title: Item 09 (2) - Statement of Accounts - App 2 - Audit Findings Report 2024-25 FINAL
findings.headline: Auditors will disclaim their opinion and cannot verify any opening balances or comparative figures
findings.detail: Due to prior-year disclaimed accounts (2020/21 to 2023/24), the Council has no assurance on opening balances for 2024/25. The auditors state: 'Due to the lack of assurance over opening balances and unresolved issues in 2023/24, a disclaimer of opinion will be issued for 2024/25. This reflects the pervasive impact of prior-year issues and limitations in obtaining sufficient audit evidence.' This means the 2023/24 comparative figures in the accounts are unaudited.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means there is no independent verification of the financial position. For a lender, this removes the standard assurance on financial statements and creates reliance on unverified opening positions spanning five years.
findings.figures: Applies to all opening balance figures; auditors unable to provide assurance on closing reserves balance due to uncertainty over their opening amount
findings.quote: Due to the lack of assurance over opening balances and unresolved issues in 2023/24, a disclaimer of opinion will be issued for 2024/25. This reflects the pervasive impact of prior-year issues and limitations in obtaining sufficient audit evidence.

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Appendix 2 - Treasury Management Strategy
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account financing costs rise to 46% of HRA net revenue by 2027-28, straining housing service delivery.
findings.detail: HRA debt service costs (interest, principal repayment, and MRP) climb from £12.3m (2023-24 actual) to £16.4m (2027-28 estimate), growing from 38% to 46% of HRA net revenue stream. The HRA self-financed debt of £184m borrowed in March 2012 remains the council's largest single liability, now at £150m. Rising costs despite declining debt principal indicates either higher interest rates on the debt mix or substantial MRP charges.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned that nearly half of HRA revenue is committed to financing costs, severely constraining investment in housing maintenance, modernisation, or service improvement, and leaving little buffer for demand shocks.
findings.figures: HRA financing costs: £12.3m (2023-24 actual) rising to £16.4m (2027-28 estimate); as % of net revenue: 38% (2023-24) to 46% (2027-28); HRA debt outstanding: £150m (2023-24 actual), declining to £110m (2027-28 estimate)
findings.quote: Housing Revenue Account 12.3 [2023-24 net income/expense] 13.3 14.3 15.3 16.4 [2027-28]; Housing Revenue Account 38% [2023-24] 38% 41% 44% 46% [2027-28]

findings.paper_title: Item 6 - Appendix 2 - Treasury Management Strategy
findings.headline: Council maintains under-borrowed position by drawing on reserves rather than external borrowing despite rising capital need.
findings.detail: Guildford is deliberately avoiding external borrowing by using cash and reserves to finance capital. The General Fund Capital Financing Requirement rises from £14m (2023-24 actual) to £40m (2027-28 estimate), but the council plans zero external borrowing across all forecast years. This under-borrowed strategy is described as temporary, prudent only while investment returns are low and counterparty risk uncertain.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand when this reserves-based strategy ends and whether the council will face forced borrowing at potentially higher rates, or face liquidity constraints.
findings.figures: General Fund CFR: £14m (2023-24) to £40m (2027-28); planned external borrowing: £0 (all years); under/over external borrowing position: -£27m to -£81m (section 2.20)
findings.quote: The Council is currently maintaining an under-borrowed position. This means that the capital borrowing need (the Capital Financing Requirement), has not been fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Council's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as a temporary measure. This strategy is prudent as treasury management investment returns are low and counterparty risk is still uncertain.
